topics: 🐐 Selling Ma'aser Behema — the meat may only be sold by 'inclusion' (havla'ah) in hide, fat, sinews, horns
🦴 Bones: Included or Not? — a dispute turning on small versus large animals, or local custom
📜 'Lo Yigael' — the Gemara chases a verbal analogy (gezeira shava) through cherem, ma'aser and bekhor
🔑 Rava's Simple Answer — cherem is either fully consecrated (with the owner) or fully non-sacred (with a priest)
🩸 Rav Ashi's Proof — 'it and its substitute' shows the prohibition applies only while the animal is alive
⚖️ The New Mishna — may a non-priest, or even a gentile, join a priest in eating a blemished firstborn?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Selling Sacred Meat, and Who May Share It
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 32a–32b
overview.hebrewSource: בִּבְכוֹר הוּא אוֹמֵר: ״לֹא יִפְדֶּה״, וְנִמְכָּר; בְּמַעֲשֵׂר נֶאֱמַר: ״לֹא יִגָּאֵל״, וְאֵינוֹ נִמְכָּר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues the discussion of the animal tithe offering (ma'aser behema) that became blemished: since Torah law says 'it shall not be redeemed' (Leviticus 27:33), its meat cannot be sold directly, only indirectly, by folding its value into the price of parts that are normally sold. The Gemara searches for the textual source of this rule, working through an elaborate chain of verbal analogies (gezeira shava) linking the tithe, dedications (cherem), and the firstborn offering, before Rava and Rav Ashi each propose their own explanation. The daf then turns to a new mishna: once a blemished firstborn belongs to a priest, may an ordinary Israelite — or even a gentile — join his household group in eating it?

slides.title: 🐐 Selling the Blemished Tithe's Meat
slides.subtitle: Bekhor vs. ma'aser: two verses, two different rules
rows: Yes — the priest may sell it directly, alive or slaughtered
Never sold directly — only by 'inclusion' (הַבְלָעָה) in its hide, fat, sinews or horns

callout.label: Orphans' exception:
callout.text: For young orphans the Sages permitted selling a blemished tithe's meat in the ordinary way, treating the rabbinic safeguard as if it did not apply, since Deuteronomy 12:15's 'blessing... after slaughter' is understood to refer specifically to the tithe.

slides.title: 🦴 Can the Meat's Value Be Folded Into the Bones?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Shimon disagree — but maybe they don't

nodes.content: ❓ May one include the meat's value in the price of the bones, the way one does with hide, fat, sinews and horns?
⚖️ Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Shimon b'Rabbi disagree: one permits, one forbids

columns.label: Reading 1
columns.content: Small animal — bones unusable, never sold, so no inclusion. Large animal — bones are sold, so inclusion works

columns.label: Reading 2
columns.content: Both discuss a large animal. Each sage simply follows the custom of his own locale about whether bones are sold there

nodes.content: ✅ Either way, the underlying rule is the same: an item never appraised while the animal was alive can absorb the tithe-meat's value once slaughtered

callout.label: Principle:
callout.text: The Sages never decreed against selling parts that were not price-factors while the animal lived; for orphans, the law is enforced as if by Torah law itself.

slides.title: 📜 Two Ways to Read 'It Shall Not Be Redeemed'
slides.subtitle: Rava and Rav Ashi each explain why the tithe's meat cannot be sold

boxes.title: Rava's Approach
items: Skips the whole gezeira-shava chain to cherem
Cherem is either fully sacred (still with the owner) or fully non-sacred (given to the priest) — never in between
So 'lo yigael' by cherem is free to teach the ma'aser's prohibition on sale directly

boxes.title: Rav Ashi's Approach
items: Reads Leviticus 27:33, 'it and its substitute... shall not be redeemed', together
Substitution (temura) only works on a live animal — so 'not redeemed' here must mean 'not redeemed', i.e. sold, while alive
After slaughter the sanctity is weaker, yet the Gemara shows by a fortiori that it must remain unsellable even then

callout.label: Why not write 'not sold' plainly?
callout.text: Had the Torah written only 'it shall not be sold,' one might think redemption (transferring sanctity to coins) remained possible. 'Lo yigael' teaches both: not sold, and not redeemed.

slides.title: 🔑 Rava's Key Move: Where Do Dedications Sit?
slides.hebrewSource: כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁהֵן בְּבֵית בְּעָלִים — הֲרֵי הֵן כְּהֶקְדֵּשׁ לְכׇל דִּבְרֵיהֶם... נְתָנָן לְכֹהֵן — הֲרֵי הֵן כְּחוּלִּין לְכׇל דִּבְרֵיהֶם
slides.label: The baraita Rava cites:
slides.text: As long as a dedicated item (cherem) sits with its owner it counts as fully consecrated (Leviticus 27:28, 'most holy to the Lord'). The moment it is handed to the priest, it becomes fully non-sacred (Numbers 18:14, 'shall be for you'). Since cherem is never in an intermediate 'redeemable' state, the phrase 'lo yigael' written about it has no local purpose — freeing it to teach, by verbal analogy, that the animal tithe's meat may not be sold.

slides.title: ⚖️ New Mishna: Who May Eat the Blemished Firstborn?
slides.subtitle: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether a non-priest — or a gentile — may join the group

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: Beit Shammai: an Israelite may not be counted together with the priest to partake of a blemished firstborn. Beit Hillel permit it — even for a gentile.

lines.speaker: Beit Shammai
lines.text: Numbers 18:18, 'their flesh shall be yours,' is compared to the priestly breast and thigh: just as an Israelite may not eat those, he may not eat this.

lines.speaker: Beit Hillel
lines.text: That verse discusses only an unblemished firstborn offered on the altar. For the blemished one, Deuteronomy 15:22 says הַטָּמֵא וְהַטָּהוֹר יַחְדָּו יֹאכְלֶנּוּ — 'the impure and the pure alike may eat it.'

lines.speaker: Beit Hillel
lines.text: A fortiori: if an impure priest — barred from lesser sacrifices — may eat the blemished firstborn, surely a non-priest, who may eat lesser sacrifices, may eat it too!

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: That inference can be refuted: impurity's general ban is sometimes lifted (impure priests may serve when no pure ones exist); a non-priest's ban on service is never lifted.

lines.speaker: Beit Hillel
lines.text: We spoke of eating, not service — and a non-priest's eating is even better suited to compare than an impure priest's.

callout.label: Rabbi Akiva's addition:
callout.text: The mishna's 'even a gentile' follows Rabbi Akiva, who derives it from 'like the gazelle and the deer' (Deuteronomy 15:22) — animals a gentile may freely eat.

summary.principle: A blemished animal tithe's meat can never be sold directly, only 'included' in parts not normally priced — but once a blemished firstborn belongs to a priest, Beit Hillel permit even a non-priest or gentile to share the meal with him.

flowSteps.content: 🐐 Ma'aser meat: 'lo yigael' bars direct sale, so its value is folded into hide, fat, sinews, horns (and sometimes bones)
📜 Gemara searches for the source: gezeira shava chasing 'lo yigael' through cherem, ma'aser and bekhor

columns.content: 🔑 Rava: cherem is always fully sacred or fully non-sacred, so its verse is free for the analogy
🩸 Rav Ashi: 'it and its substitute' shows the ban applies while alive, proven further by a fortiori

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ New mishna: Beit Shammai bar non-priests from the blemished firstborn meal; Beit Hillel permit even gentiles
🎓 Key Principle: 'Lo yigael' forbids both sale and redemption of the tithe; the blemished firstborn's table is open wider than sacrificial meat generally is

quiz.q: How may the meat of a blemished animal tithe offering be sold, according to the baraita?
o: It may be sold directly like ordinary meat
Only by including its value in the price of parts like the hide, fat, sinews, or horns
It may never be sold under any circumstance
Only to a priest
quiz.e: Because 'it shall not be redeemed' bars direct sale, the meat's value is folded (havla'ah) into parts not normally appraised while the animal was alive.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the firstborn offering (bekhor) from the animal tithe (ma'aser) regarding sale of the meat?
o: They are identical in every respect
The firstborn's meat may be sold directly by the priest; the tithe's may only be sold by inclusion
The tithe may be sold directly; the firstborn may not
Neither may ever be sold
quiz.e: Numbers 18:17 ('you shall not redeem') permits the priest to sell a firstborn directly, while Leviticus 27:33 ('it shall not be redeemed') bars direct sale of the tithe.

quiz.q: According to Rava, why is the phrase 'lo yigael' written regarding dedications (cherem) available to teach the law of the animal tithe by verbal analogy?
o: Because cherem has no sanctity at all
Because cherem is always either fully consecrated (with the owner) or fully non-sacred (with the priest), never in a redeemable in-between state
Because cherem can always be redeemed
Because the Torah never mentions cherem elsewhere
quiz.e: Rava explains that since cherem is never in an intermediate, redeemable status, the verse's use of 'lo yigael' there is 'free' (a superfluous term) and can be applied by analogy to the tithe.

quiz.q: What does Rav Ashi derive from Leviticus 27:33, 'it and its substitute shall be holy; it shall not be redeemed'?
o: That the tithe may always be redeemed after slaughter
That the prohibition applies only while the animal is alive, since substitution (temura) only works on a living animal — yet a fortiori it stays unsellable even after slaughter
That substitution can happen after slaughter too
That the verse has no legal implication
quiz.e: Since temura only functions on a live animal, 'not redeemed' in that clause must refer to the live animal; Rav Ashi then shows by a fortiori reasoning that the restriction continues even after slaughter.

quiz.q: In the new mishna, what do Beit Hillel rule about who may join a priest in eating a blemished firstborn?
o: Only priests may partake
Only priests and their wives
A non-priest may partake, and Rabbi Akiva's version adds that even a gentile may
No one may eat it at all
quiz.e: Beit Hillel permit even a non-priest to join the meal, reasoning a fortiori from an impure priest's right to eat it; Rabbi Akiva extends this to a gentile via 'like the gazelle and the deer.'
